Photograph: Posed by model; dotdotred/Getty Images/Image Source Swimming Wild swimming linked to higher risk of stomach bugs and skin rashes Findings from research into illnesses associated with bathing in lakes and rivers come amid boom in hobby Matthew Pearce Thu 27 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Wild swimming has been linked to a higher risk of stomach bugs and skin rashes, according to the largest ever controlled study of illnesses associated with bathing in rivers and lakes. The research found that swimmers at locations in Hungary were more than twice as likely to develop skin problems, while the risk of contracting a stomach bug rose significantly in water with higher concentrations of E coli and other bacteria linked to faecal pollution. The findings raise questions about the World Health Organization’s decision to drop E coli as a recommended indicator of pollution in freshwater bathing sites, amid growing public concern over water quality and a boom in outdoor swimming . Paul Hunter, a professor of medicine at the University of East Anglia , who led the study, said: “The original guidelines, which were published in about 2003 – and I was part of the group that developed those – recommended [monitoring of] both E coli and enterococci for marine and fresh waters. “WHO produced new guidelines , and they basically said: ‘Don’t worry about E coli , just focus on enterococci.’ Rather embarrassingly, what we found is that enterococci aren’t associated with increased risk, but E coli is.” The study involved 2,368 people at two river and two lake-like bathing sites in Hungary . Participants were randomly allocated either to spend 10 minutes in the water, immersing their face at least three times, or to remain on the shore without entering it. Water was sampled throughout the trials, allowing researchers to estimate each swimmer’s exposure to E coli , intestinal enterococci and somatic coliphages – viruses that infect bacteria and can indicate faecal contamination. Participants were questioned about symptoms a week later. About 2.1% of swimmers reported gastrointestinal illness, including diarrhoea, vomiting or nausea accompanied by fever, compared with 1.9% of non-swimmers. Swimmers warned of toxic algae at newly designated Thames bathing site Read more Although bathing alone was not statistically linked to stomach illness, the risk increased significantly among swimmers exposed to higher concentrations of E coli and coliphages. Skin complaints, defined as a rash, ulcer or itching, were reported by 2.7% of swimmers and 1.3% of people who stayed out of the water, making bathers more than twice as likely to develop a skin ailment. Hunter said he was “fairly confident” that the findings would be applicable to the UK despite the research being conducted in Hungary. A separate German study in 2006 produced similar results. He added: “We have two different countries with essentially the same findings, Germany and Hungary, and climatically they are not that different to us in many ways.” The skin problems reported were not associated with any of the three measures of faecal contamination, suggesting other organisms or pollutants may have been responsible. “People going into fresh waters do have an increased risk of skin irritation,” Hunter said. “We don’t know what is causing that. One explanation is something called cercarial dermatitis, where avian parasites burrow into human skin and cause a reaction. Irritation from algae in rivers and lakes might also be causing it. “But that is speculation: what we do know is that the skin irritation is not related to markers of faecal pollution.” Cases of respiratory, ear and eye infections were also more frequent among swimmers, but the numbers were too small for researchers to draw any reliable conclusions. All four sites complied with EU bathing-water standards that were in force when the trials took place. The researchers said the randomised design provided stronger evidence than observational studies. However, they cautioned that the results were based on a single trial day at each site and that some participants reported swimming elsewhere during the study period. Hunter said the results supported retaining E coli in freshwater monitoring and suggested somatic coliphages could also help identify unsafe conditions. “I think there is a very strong argument that E coli , particularly for fresh waters rather than marine waters, should be part of the standards and should be part of the guidelines,” he added. Home > Arts News > UNO Jazz Takes Learning Beyond the Classroom By Michael Hilt UNO Jazz Takes Learning Beyond the Classroom September 14th, 2026 Download For students in the University of Nebraska at Omaha’s jazz program, some of the most valuable lessons happen far beyond the classroom. Pete Madsen, a longtime professor in the UNO School of Music, has helped make travel and live performance an important part of the student experience. Madsen teaches trombone, oversees the music graduate program and serves as coordinator of Jazz Studies, an area that has experienced significant growth during his time at the university. Touring has played an important role in that growth. UNO jazz students have had opportunities to perform regionally, nationally and internationally, gaining experience in front of new audiences while learning what it takes to perform consistently from one venue to another. That work is also bringing national recognition to the program. UNO Jazz has been invited to perform at the Jazz Education Network Conference in January, giving students the opportunity to represent the university at a major gathering of jazz musicians and educators. For Madsen, however, student tours are about much more than performances. They are educational experiences designed to expose students to different cultures, musicians and ways of understanding the world. That will be especially evident during a September trip to Latvia and Lithuania. International travel gives students the opportunity to experience music within a different cultural environment while also using their own performances as a form of cultural exchange. Madsen sees music as a powerful part of society and an important way for people from different backgrounds to communicate and connect. That perspective has helped shape his approach to jazz education at UNO. As he begins his 27th year at the university, Madsen has watched the jazz program and its opportunities expand in ways he could not have imagined when he first arrived on campus. For him, the most meaningful part of that growth is what it provides for students. Touring can introduce young musicians to places they have never visited, audiences they have never performed for and, in some cases, their first experience traveling outside the United States. Those experiences become part of an education that extends well beyond learning notes, technique and repertoire — giving students a chance to discover more about music, the world and themselves. share tweet Next Post ArteLatinX Celebrates Hispanic Heritage With 10th Annual Arts Exhibition ArteLatinX celebrates its 10th anniversary with an art exhibition, workshops, and guest speakers showcasing Latino art and culture across the Great Plains.

https://www.dw.com/en/latvia-election-pr.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ngfd Centrist Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (right) is on track for a strong win in the elections Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP Advertisement Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs appeared set to remain in power on Sunday after his centrist United List secured 35.3% of the vote in the country's parliamentary election. The result gives United List 42 of 100 seats and puts Kulbergs in a strong position to form another pro-Ukraine coalition. What do the results show? With 97% of ballots counted, United List had secured the country's biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991. The party could secure a parliamentary majority with either the nationalist National Alliance or the left-leaning Progressives, political scientist Roberts Kits said. Kulbergs, a 47-year-old businessman and amateur rally driver, only came to power in May after the previous coalition collapsed over its handling of incidents involving stray Ukrainian military drones. Latvia vote shaped by Russia fears To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video An exit poll put the the populist Latvia First party in second place with 11.3% — nearly double its share at the last election in 2022. It had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority. Kulbergs said on Saturday night that he would not cooperate with any pro-Russian parties and specifically ruled out forming a coaltition with Latvia First. Some 1.5 million people were eligible to vote in the country's 11th parliamentary election since independence in 1991. The election, which saw 100 seats in the Saeima being contested by 14 parties using a proportional system, was dominated by rising living costs and national security concerns in the small Baltic country which borders both Russia and Belarus . Latvia vote shaped by Russia concerns Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine is seen as a direct threat to national security in Latvia which, like Ukraine, is a former Soviet state with a sizeable ethnic Russian and Russian-speaking minority. Unlike Ukraine , however, Latvia is a member of both the European Union and NATO . Riga is one of Kyiv's closest partners and supporters, having committed itself by law to spending at least 5% of GDP on defense – leaving less room for spending elsewhere. Many Latvians complain of high prices and low wages, the economy is sluggish, the health system is under strain, and emigration and an ageing population remain persistent challenges. Populist movements such as the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and the Latvia First party have attempted to exploit discontent by taking a less stringent line towards Moscow and arguing that a complete economic decoupling from Russia is damaging. Indeed, four German Eurofighter jets were deployed to protect Latvian airspace during the election in response to a request from Riga. https://www.chronicle.lu/category/intern.text: Home News International News Latvians Vote in Election in Shadow of Drone Incursions & War in Ukraine Latvians Vote in Election in Shadow of Drone Incursions & War in Ukraine Published on Saturday, 03 Oct 2026 09:49 by EO Share This Article: Rate this item: "Unites List" election campaign poster featuring Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs before the general election in Riga, Latvia, 27 September 2026. Sign reads "Kulbergs is the solution"; Credit: REUTERS/Ints Kalnins RIGA (Reuters) - Latvians vote in a parliamentary election on Saturday 3 October 2026 that is likely to keep power in the hands of pro-Ukrainian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, although deep political fragmentation may complicate the formation of a government. Across the Baltics, including in NATO and European Union member Latvia, many voters are on edge after official warnings of potential Russian aggression and a growing number of airspace incursions related to Moscow's war in Ukraine. Russia says accusations that it is planning to attack NATO are baseless and Western officials say it is not capable of launching a direct assault, but security concerns have weighed heavily in the election campaign. Opinion polls put Kulbergs' centrist United List ahead, with about 14% of votes, but followed closely by the overtly pro-Russian Sovereign Power. A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May 2026 after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray military drones flew undetected into Latvia. Though the drones were Ukrainian, officials have blamed Russia for causing them to divert from their flight paths. " We have to give Ukraine everything necessary right now (so) that they can have the upper hand and win ," Kulbergs told Reuters in an interview last month. Throughout his campaign, he has also promised more anti-drone capabilities for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5% of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels in NATO. But his pro-Kremlin rivals say Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and should instead focus more on cost-of-living issues, particularly among his country's Russian-speaking minority. " Our voters want peace, to stop looking for shelters, to no longer experience the air alerts ," party leader Julia Stepanenko told Reuters. " The war must not be encouraged in any way, including by financing it... Ukraine must win, but through peace talks ." Polls open at 08:00 (0500 GMT) on Saturday and close at 20:00, with the first results expected within hours and the final result likely to be clear after midnight. The 100 members of the Saeima, or parliament, are being elected for a four-year term. Divided nation Surveys show at least two other parties may make it into parliament - the populist, MAGA-style Latvia First grouping and the Progressives, a left-leaning party that attracts younger voters. Kulbergs' ability to forge a working coalition will depend largely on how many votes they receive and how many other parties cross the 5% threshold to enter parliament. He might also need to cobble together a deal with Latvia First leader, businessman Ainars Slesers, who appears to have shifted towards a more anti-Ukraine stance in recent months, courting votes on both sides. " His message is that (the party) condemns Russia's invasion and stands with Ukraine, but that supporting Ukraine comes at the expense of Latvia's economy ," said Roberts Kits, researcher for the Latvian Strategy and Economic Research Institute, in a note. Latvia, with a population of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea, with EU and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south, and Russia and Belarus to the east.
